Date:   Mon Sep 21 15:32:40 2026 +0300

    fix(canvas): a tile the library never measured has no arrows drawn to it
    
    **The root.** A wire is drawn between two handles, and where a handle sits
    inside a tile is something the drawing library measures — through the same
    `ResizeObserver` notification a busy browser abandons when too many fall due in
    one frame. #37 met that as tiles that never appeared and fixed it by telling
    the library each tile's box outright; a box is not a handle, so the wire half
    was left. An abandoned notification is never delivered, so the arrow stays off
    the glass for the life of the page.
    
    **Measured three ways.** Drop every tile's notification and keep the glass's:
    seven tiles drawn, none hidden, twenty-eight handles on the glass, and not one
    arrow. Drop only the insurance premium's: the two arrows touching it go, and
    only those. Drop only the strait's: its three go. And in the wild, on ports
    nobody else on this machine held, with the fix reverted and sixteen busy loops
    alongside — one run in two hundred at six workers lost `H->C` exactly that way,
    with every tile in place.
    
    `useHandlesTheLibraryHasMeasured` asks the library to measure again and keeps
    asking until it says it has. `nodesInitialized` is that fact — false until every
    tile has handle bounds — so this acts on the state of the map rather than on a
    guess about timing, and asking is a direct measurement rather than another
    notification to be dropped. It is a timer rather than an animation frame
    because a browser produces no frames while nothing is changing, and nothing
    changing is precisely the fault; #37 learnt that one the hard way.
    
    The end-to-end helper no longer waits a missing arrow out. It asserts the arrow
    is there and names it, so a return of this fails in fifteen seconds instead of
    forty-five.

1	/**
2	 * How big a tile is, and how far the map may be zoomed.
3	 *
4	 * The automatic layout has to know how big every tile is *before* the browser
5	 * has drawn one — it works out where the tiles go from the shape of the map
6	 * alone, and it cannot wait for measurements. So a tile's height is computed
7	 * here, from the claim's own content, by a plain function of plain data. That
8	 * keeps the layout a pure function of the map: the same map lays out the same
9	 * way every time, and the layout can be tested without a browser.
10	 *
11	 * The block heights below were measured once in the browser against the stored
12	 * example and are written down rather than read back at run time. If the tile's
13	 * stylesheet changes a line height or a gap, these change with it — and the
14	 * check for that is visual: a tile whose numbers are wrong has a gap at the
15	 * bottom or loses its last line.
16	 */
17	
18	import type { ClaimView } from "../world";
19	
20	/** How wide a tile is. Settled: 280 pixels, and measurable on any screenshot. */
21	export const TILE_WIDTH = 280;
22	
23	/**
24	 * How tall a tile may be, at the least and at the most.
25	 *
26	 * "Clamped height" is a floor and a ceiling with the content deciding in
27	 * between — not one height for every tile. The floor is what a tile holding
28	 * only a heading, a one-line claim and the three belief chips comes to; the
29	 * ceiling is what the densest tile in the stored example needs, which is the
30	 * hypothesis, with a three-line claim, a reason and two evidence clippings.
31	 * Both are on the eight-pixel grid.
32	 */
33	export const TILE_MIN_HEIGHT = 152;
34	/**
35	 * The ceiling was 272, which was what the densest tile in the stored example
36	 * needed **before a tile could carry badges**. A claim the reader supposed and a
37	 * later edit pushed back down says so on its own face, in one line that names
38	 * the edit responsible — *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed
39	 * military strike on Iranian territory"* — and that line is three lines wide on
40	 * a 280-pixel tile. A ceiling that cut it off would hide the one thing the tile
41	 * is there to say.
42	 */
43	export const TILE_MAX_HEIGHT = 320;
44	
45	/* ---- The blocks a tile is made of, in pixels --------------------------- *
46	 * Measured in the browser, at the type sizes and line heights `tile.css`
47	 * sets. Every one of them is a height the browser actually produced. */
48	
49	/** Top and bottom padding together: twelve pixels each. */
50	const PADDING = 24;
51	
52	/** The gap between one block and the next. */
53	const GAP = 8;
54	
55	/** The heading row: what kind of claim this is, and when it settles. */
56	const HEADER = 21;
57	
58	/**
59	 * One line of the claim, at fifteen pixels over a line height of 1.35.
60	 *
61	 * Rounded up wherever it is used, never down: a line that is given a quarter of
62	 * a pixel less than it needs loses the bottom of its descenders.
63	 */
64	const CLAIM_LINE = 20.25;
65	
66	/**
67	 * The three belief chips: owner, number and range, with the rule above them.
68	 *
69	 * Measured at 69 in the browser, which is two pixels more than the 67 written
70	 * here before the chips grew their brightness bars. A row that is two pixels
71	 * short takes them off the bottom of the tile.
72	 */
73	const BELIEF_RAIL = 69;
74	
75	/**
76	 * The line a dead end prints saying why nothing here can be traded. Clamped to
77	 * two lines, and the only reason any tile prints for itself.
78	 */
79	const FINDING = 35;
80	
81	/** One evidence clipping, and the gap between two of them. */
82	const CLIPPING = 21;
83	const CLIPPING_GAP = 4;
84	
85	/**
86	 * One line of a claim's badges, and the hairline and padding the badges
87	 * themselves add to the block once.
88	 *
89	 * Thirteen pixels over a line height of 1.35 is 17.5, and each badge is drawn
90	 * with a hairline round it and a pixel of padding, which lifts a line box to
91	 * about 19. Both measured in the browser against the stored example's strike
92	 * branch, where the tallest badge line in the product — *Supposed · Oct 1 →
93	 * Retracted · Oct 2 · by "…"* — runs to three lines.
94	 */
95	const BADGE_LINE = 19;
96	const BADGE_PADDING = 4;
97	
98	/**
99	 * Roughly how many characters of a badge fit on one line.
100	 *
101	 * The badges flow across the same 256 pixels the claim wraps in, set at thirteen
102	 * pixels in the interface face, whose average character is about six and a half
103	 * pixels wide — so about thirty-eight. An estimate, and safe to be one for the
104	 * same reason the claim's is: the same number decides both how tall the tile is
105	 * and how much room the badges get, so the two cannot disagree.
106	 */
107	const BADGE_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE = 38;
108	
109	/** The separator drawn between one badge and the next, counted into the width. */
110	const BADGE_SEPARATOR = " → ";
111	
112	/**
113	 * Roughly how many characters of the claim fit on one line.
114	 *
115	 * The claim has 256 pixels to wrap in (244 on the two tiles whose outline cuts
116	 * into one side) and is set at fifteen pixels in the interface face, whose
117	 * average character is about eight pixels wide — so about thirty-three.
118	 *
119	 * It is an estimate, and it is safe to be one because the same number decides
120	 * both how tall the tile is and how many lines the claim is allowed to show.
121	 * The two cannot disagree: if the estimate is generous the tile has a little
122	 * room to spare, and if it is mean the claim stops one line earlier than it
123	 * might have. Neither case can push a word out of the box.
124	 */
125	const CLAIM_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE = 33;
126	
127	/** The most lines of the claim a tile ever shows. The rest lives in the panel. */
128	const CLAIM_MAX_LINES = 3;
129	
130	/**
131	 * How many lines of the claim this tile shows.
132	 *
133	 * @param claim The claim, in the words the map serves it in.
134	 */
135	export function claimLines(claim: string): number {
136	  const wanted = Math.ceil(claim.length / CLAIM_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE);
137	  return Math.min(CLAIM_MAX_LINES, Math.max(1, wanted));
138	}
139	
140	/**
141	 * How many lines this claim's badges take.
142	 *
143	 * Zero when it has none, which is every claim on a map nobody has edited.
144	 *
145	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
146	 */
147	export function badgeLines(claim: ClaimView): number {
148	  const badges = claim.badges ?? [];
149	  if (badges.length === 0) {
150	    return 0;
151	  }
152	  const characters =
153	    badges.reduce((sum, badge) => sum + badge.words.length, 0) +
154	    BADGE_SEPARATOR.length * (badges.length - 1);
155	  return Math.max(1, Math.ceil(characters / BADGE_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE));
156	}
157	
158	/** Round up to the eight-pixel grid the whole interface sits on. */
159	function toGrid(height: number): number {
160	  return Math.ceil(height / 8) * 8;
161	}
162	
163	/**
164	 * How tall this claim's tile wants to be, before the grid, the floor and the
165	 * ceiling are put to it.
166	 *
167	 * Kept apart from the bounding below because a height that has been bounded is
168	 * no longer a height you can do arithmetic with: two clamped numbers added
169	 * together can land outside the very bounds each of them was clamped into.
170	 *
171	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
172	 * @param badges How many lines the badges take. Passed in rather than read off
173	 *   the claim so that a caller reserving a line of its own for one badge can
174	 *   say so without building a second claim to say it with.
175	 */
176	function naturalHeight(claim: ClaimView, badges: number): number {
177	  const blocks: number[] = [HEADER, Math.ceil(CLAIM_LINE * claimLines(claim.claim)), BELIEF_RAIL];
178	
179	  // The foot of the tile: the reason a slot has no number, and the evidence
180	  // clippings. It is only there when there is something to put in it — and
181	  // when the badges arrive, having one of those will put it there too.
182	  const foot: number[] = [];
183	  if (claim.kind === "not_tradeable" && claim.beliefs.market.absence !== undefined) {
184	    foot.push(FINDING);
185	  }
186	  const clippings = claim.evidence.length;
187	  if (clippings > 0) {
188	    foot.push(CLIPPING * clippings + CLIPPING_GAP * (clippings - 1));
189	  }
190	  if (badges > 0) {
191	    foot.push(BADGE_LINE * badges + BADGE_PADDING);
192	  }
193	  if (foot.length > 0) {
194	    blocks.push(foot.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + GAP * (foot.length - 1));
195	  }
196	
197	  return PADDING + blocks.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + GAP * (blocks.length - 1);
198	}
199	
200	/** Put a wanted height on the eight-pixel grid, inside the floor and the ceiling. */
201	function bounded(natural: number): number {
202	  return Math.min(TILE_MAX_HEIGHT, Math.max(TILE_MIN_HEIGHT, toGrid(natural)));
203	}
204	
205	/**
206	 * How tall this claim's tile is: as tall as its own content, on the grid, and
207	 * inside the floor and the ceiling.
208	 *
209	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
210	 */
211	export function tileHeight(claim: ClaimView): number {
212	  return bounded(naturalHeight(claim, badgeLines(claim)));
213	}
214	
215	/**
216	 * How tall a box this claim's tile needs when how far its number moved gets a
217	 * line of its own.
218	 *
219	 * A tile is as tall as its own content, and the layout has to know that before
220	 * the browser has drawn one — so the height is a plain function of the claim.
221	 * This adds one thing to it: **the movement line is not packed in with whatever
222	 * the edits had to say.** On the busiest tile on the map, *Supposed · Oct 1 →
223	 * Retracted · Oct 2 · by "…"* already runs to three lines, and stringing a
224	 * reading on the end of that run pushes a line out of the box.
225	 *
226	 * The extra line is measured rather than written down — the words and the
227	 * reading are each measured on their own — so if the badge line height ever
228	 * changes, this changes with it.
229	 *
230	 * **The wanted height is worked out once and bounded once.** This was first
231	 * written as three already-bounded heights added and subtracted — with the
232	 * badges, with the reading, less the empty tile — and a bounded height is not a
233	 * number to do arithmetic with. The floor is added twice and taken off once, so
234	 * an ordinary tile is handed more room than its content needs (the busiest tile
235	 * on the stored example: 296 pixels reserved against the 280 it wants), and
236	 * nothing holds the total under the ceiling that each of the three was clamped
237	 * into.
238	 *
239	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
240	 */
241	export function roomFor(claim: ClaimView): number {
242	  const badges = claim.badges ?? [];
243	  const said = badges.filter((badge) => badge.movement !== true);
244	  const moved = badges.filter((badge) => badge.movement === true);
245	  const lines =
246	    said.length === 0 || moved.length === 0
247	      ? badgeLines(claim)
248	      : badgeLines({ ...claim, badges: said }) + badgeLines({ ...claim, badges: moved });
249	  return bounded(naturalHeight(claim, lines));
250	}
251	
252	/* ---- Zoom --------------------------------------------------------------- */
253	
254	/**
255	 * The smallest a word may be drawn on the reader's screen, in pixels.
256	 *
257	 * This is the rule the two zoom numbers below are worked out from, rather than
258	 * a number chosen for how it looked.
259	 */
260	const SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT = 11;
261	
262	/** The smallest and largest of the three type sizes, as `tokens.css` sets them. */
263	const SMALLEST_TEXT = 13;
264	const LARGEST_TEXT = 22;
265	
266	/**
267	 * Below this zoom a tile stops showing everything and shows a summary instead.
268	 *
269	 * **This was 0.6, and it is now eleven over thirteen — about 0.85.** The plan
270	 * settled on 0.6 before the type scale was settled, and the two turned out not
271	 * to fit together: a full tile's smallest words are thirteen pixels, so at 0.6
272	 * zoom they arrive on the glass at under eight, which breaks the rule that
273	 * nothing is ever drawn below eleven. Eleven over thirteen is the exact zoom at
274	 * which thirteen-pixel type lands at eleven pixels, so a full tile is only ever
275	 * shown at or above it, and below it the summary takes over — which sets every
276	 * word in the largest size and so clears the floor all the way down.
277	 */
278	export const SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT / SMALLEST_TEXT;
279	
280	/**
281	 * How far out the map may be zoomed.
282	 *
283	 * The summary sets every word it draws in the largest of the three type sizes,
284	 * so the floor is the one zoom at which that size arrives at eleven pixels:
285	 * eleven over twenty-two, which is a half.
286	 */
287	export const SMALLEST_ZOOM = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT / LARGEST_TEXT;
288	
289	/** How far in the map may be zoomed. Past this a tile is merely large. */
290	export const LARGEST_ZOOM = 1.4;
291	
292	/**
293	 * The smallest type size a tile draws at this zoom, in pixels, before the map's
294	 * own scaling is applied.
295	 *
296	 * Multiply it by the zoom and you have what lands on the reader's screen, which
297	 * is what `layout.test.ts` checks never falls below eleven.
298	 *
299	 * @param zoom How far the map is zoomed in, where 1 is life size.
300	 */
301	export function smallestTextAt(zoom: number): number {
302	  return zoom < SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM ? LARGEST_TEXT : SMALLEST_TEXT;
303	}
304	
305	/** The smallest a word is ever drawn on the reader's screen, in pixels. */
306	export const TEXT_FLOOR = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT;
307	
308	/* ---- The first frame ----------------------------------------------------- */
309	
310	/** A rectangle in the map's own coordinates. */
311	export interface Box {
312	  readonly x: number;
313	  readonly y: number;
314	  readonly width: number;
315	  readonly height: number;
316	}
317	
318	/** How far the map is moved and zoomed to put something in front of the reader. */
319	export interface Frame {
320	  /** How far in the map is zoomed, where 1 is life size. */
321	  readonly zoom: number;
322	  /** How far the map is slid sideways, in screen pixels. */
323	  readonly x: number;
324	  /** How far the map is slid up or down, in screen pixels. */
325	  readonly y: number;
326	}
327	
328	/** The breathing room left around the map when it is framed, as a share of its size. */
329	const FIRST_FRAME_MARGIN = 0.04;
330	
331	/** The gap left at the edge when the map is too big to fit and has to be panned. */
332	const EDGE_GAP = 16;
333	
334	/**
335	 * How the map is framed the first time it is drawn — and the one promise that
336	 * framing makes: **the first frame never shows summary tiles.**
337	 *
338	 * The obvious rule is "fit the whole map". On a wide screen with the panel beside
339	 * it that lands at about 0.8 zoom on the stored example, which is under the zoom
340	 * at which a full tile's smallest words would be drawn below eleven pixels — so
341	 * every tile would open as a summary, and the reader's first sight of the
342	 * product would be seven boxes with a headline and three numbers in them.
343	 *
344	 * So the rule has a floor, and the floor is the same eleven-pixel rule
345	 * everything else here is derived from: frame the whole map if it fits at a
346	 * readable size, and if it does not, keep the readable size and start at the
347	 * map's beginning, on the left, where the hypothesis is. The reader pans to the
348	 * rest. A tile changes representation rather than shrinking; the same principle,
349	 * applied to the frame rather than to the tile.
350	 *
351	 * @param map Everything the frame has to hold, in the map's own coordinates.
352	 * @param canvas How much room there is for it, in screen pixels.
353	 */
354	export function firstFrame(map: Box, canvas: { width: number; height: number }): Frame {
355	  const fits = Math.min(
356	    canvas.width / (map.width * (1 + FIRST_FRAME_MARGIN)),
357	    canvas.height / (map.height * (1 + FIRST_FRAME_MARGIN)),
358	  );
359	  // Never blown up past life size, however small the map; never shrunk past the
360	  // point where a full tile would have to become a summary.
361	  const zoom = Math.max(SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM, Math.min(1, fits));
362	  const place = (room: number, start: number, size: number): number => {
363	    const shown = size * zoom;
364	    return shown <= room ? (room - shown) / 2 - start * zoom : EDGE_GAP - start * zoom;
365	  };
366	  return {
367	    zoom,
368	    x: place(canvas.width, map.x, map.width),
369	    y: place(canvas.height, map.y, map.height),
370	  };
371	}
372	
373	/** How many tiles a single layer may show before the rest are collapsed into one. */
374	export const TILES_PER_LAYER = 7;
375

/**
 * The one end-to-end test: the stored example, opened and edited, **by keyboard
 * alone**.
 *
 * It is the only test in this product that drives a real browser against a real
 * server, so it is spent on the one claim nothing else can make: that the two
 * halves, started the way a person starts them, draw the stored example — and
 * that the three things the interface exists to say are on the screen.
 *
 * 1. **The map draws, with the engine's own numbers**, from the server's own
 *    copy of the example. Nothing on it is typed into the browser — and nothing
 *    is typed into this file either: every number below is compared with itself
 *    across a change, or checked for its shape, never for its value.
 * 2. **Opening the strike branch moves the numbers, and OPEC+'s announcement
 *    does not move.** That is the product's central correctness claim — *here is
 *    what your edit can reach, and here is what it provably cannot* — and it is
 *    checked here against the engine's own answer rather than against a shape a
 *    test wrote out. It is also where the browser's structural reading and the
 *    engine's meet: the browser is what puts *untouched* on OPEC's announcement,
 *    and the engine is what leaves its number where it was.
 * 3. **The hypothesis says its supposition was overridden**, word for word:
 *    *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed military strike on
 *    Iranian territory"* — read off the world the engine built.
 *
 * **The whole walk is done with the keyboard**, and that is not a flourish: it
 * is the check that the interface is usable without a mouse end to end. Every
 * step below is a keystroke a reader could make.
 *
 * It needs no model key. The screen it drives is fed by a stored example, which
 * calls nothing.
 */

import { expect, type Locator, type Page, test } from "@playwright/test";

/*
 * ---- Waiting, and why every read below does it --------------------------
 *
 * **Nothing here reads a value the page has not settled on.** This test drives
 * two servers, a background layout thread and a drawing library that measures
 * its own boxes, so at any moment the screen may be showing the answer to the
 * question before last. Every read goes through one of the helpers below, and
 * each of them waits for a *named* signal rather than for a number of
 * milliseconds — a sleep is a guess, and the build machine is about two and a
 * half times slower than the machine it was guessed on.
 *
 * Two traps in particular are what these exist for.
 *
 * **`innerText` is not `textContent`.** `innerText` is what the page *renders*,
 * so it comes back empty for a tile the drawing library has not measured yet —
 * which is how a chip that plainly reads `.19` was read as `""`. Nothing below
 * calls `innerText`; the reads wait for the element to be visible and then take
 * `textContent`, which is the same string by then.
 *
 * **The old numbers stay on screen until the new ones arrive.** An edit asks
 * for a whole new world and a whole new difference, and until they come back
 * the map is still drawing the previous answer. So waiting for *a* number is
 * not waiting: each edit below waits for the thing that **changes** — the
 * sentence the map says out loud for that edit — before anything is read.
 */

tiles-ports-wires.md:1:# Tiles, ports and wires — what a claim and an arrow look like
tiles-ports-wires.md:5:A claim and an arrow are the two things the whole product is made of, and until now they have only existed as data shapes. This chapter turns them into objects you can look at. A **tile** is a claim you can read without opening anything: what it says, who thinks it is how likely, what is behind it, and by when we will know. A **wire** is one arrow whose picture already tells you what kind of push it is, how hard it pushes, whether it holds or fires once, and whether anybody fetched a document before drawing it. A **port** is where a wire attaches, and it is typed, so what a wire means is visible at the socket before you follow it anywhere.
tiles-ports-wires.md:7:What a user can do that they could not before: glance at a map and see which step is weakly supported, which arrows are the model talking and which have something behind them, and which claim is being taken as given rather than computed — all without a click, and all without a single colour doing two jobs.

tiles-ports-wires.md:93:| 3 | **Evidence clippings** | At most two. Each is a **letter monogram** plus one line: monogram in `--font-mono`, `--weight-semibold`, `--text-muted`; line in `--font-interface`, `--text-sm`, `--text-muted`, one line, ellipsized. A leading `+` or `−` says whether the item supports the claim or cuts against it |
tiles-ports-wires.md:170:And one state that replaces the number entirely: **while an edit has fixed a claim's value, the chip shows the word** — *Supposed · Oct 1* where the user took it as given, *Happened · Oct 1* where they reported it as news, *Did not happen · Oct 1* where the news is that it did not (Kent, 2026-09-21, G12) — never `1.0`, never `.98` and never `>.99`. Either way the claim is settled in every simulated world, so there is no number to show, and inventing one would answer a question the user did not ask. (The engine stores `1.0` on such a claim — or `0.0` where the value fixed was false — so the path product has a factor to multiply; no surface but the path product ever reads it.)
tiles-ports-wires.md:174:### Typed ports
tiles-ports-wires.md:281:`--surface-raised` and `--hairline` for the tile · `--text`, `--text-muted` for every word · `--font-interface`, `--font-mono` and the three sizes and three weights · `--space-hair` through `--space-3` and `--radius` for the geometry · `--p-0` … `--p-4` for a chip's likelihood bar · `--focus` for the keyboard ring · `--duration-fast` for every opacity change. No component here reads `--dir-up`, `--dir-down` or `--tail`: a tile has no financial direction to report in this stack, and nothing on the map says which claim is a tail without arithmetic.
tiles-ports-wires.md:301:Two evidence clippings, each a monogram and a line: **B** `+ An Omani-mediated round is reported, with both sides attending.` and **L** `− Three tankers remain held and no release has been announced.` Then the resolve-by date, 1 November 2026 — the day we will know. tiles-ports-wires.md:346:### B7 — ports say what a wire means before you follow it

content.content:
And one state that replaces the number entirely: **while an edit has fixed a claim's value, the chip shows the word** — *Supposed · Oct 1* where the user took it as given, *Happened · Oct 1* where they reported it as news, *Did not happen · Oct 1* where the news is that it did not (Kent, 2026-09-21, G12) — never `1.0`, never `.98` and never `>.99`. Either way the claim is settled in every simulated world, so there is no number to show, and inventing one would answer a question the user did not ask. (The engine stores `1.0` on such a claim — or `0.0` where the value fixed was false — so the path product has a factor to multiply; no surface but the path product ever reads it.)

**The two are read from different places on the world, and that is the engine's shape rather than a quirk of ours.** A supposition can be undermined by a later edit, so whether it still holds is a fact about a *day*: the world's `states` carry it, and H reads *supposed* on the first of October and *pushed* by the day it is judged. News cannot be taken back — nothing undoes "this happened" — so it holds across the whole window and the world records it among the values its edits fixed.

### Typed ports

One **input group** and one **output group** per tile, drawn as small sockets on the left and right edges. Within each group, `trigger` and `sustain` attach to **distinct handle identifiers** — `in-trigger`, `in-sustain`, `out-trigger`, `out-sustain` *(names proposed here; that the identifiers are distinct is settled, what they are called is not)* — so a wire's meaning is visible at the socket before you follow it. `trigger` is a domino — it fires once when its cause becomes true and the effect stays pushed, fading on its own. `sustain` is an apple on a desk — the push exists only while its cause holds, and vanishes the moment it stops.

### The wire, and its five encodings

```ts
interface WireProps {
  id: string;                    // "H->B" — the two ends joined by an arrow drawn in text
  shape: "impulse" | "step" | "ramp";
  strength: number;              // signed, full precision
  mode: "trigger" | "sustain";
  reflexive: boolean;
  lagDays: number;
  provenance: "asserted" | "argued" | "documented" | "market_implied"
            | "user" | "historical" | "simulated";
  /** The conditional likelihood, when the engine has been asked for one. Absent in this stack. */
  conditional: Known<BeliefView>;
  dimmed: boolean;
}
```

A wire is a custom *edge type* — React Flow's own word for the component that draws a connection between two tiles — built on `getSmoothStepPath`, with a midpoint chip placed through `EdgeLabelRenderer`. Our word for it on screen is always **wire**. **The stroke says one thing and one thing only: what kind of push this is.**

| What | How it is drawn | Reads in greyscale |
|---|---|---|
| **Signal shape** | Stroke pattern: `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` a gradient along the stroke | Pattern |
=== B7 ===

1	/**
2	 * The map: tiles, wires, panning and zooming.
3	 *
4	 * The drawing library owns four things and no more — panning, zooming, working
5	 * out what is under the pointer, and joining two ports with a stroke. It is not
6	 * told to find those ports: where each one sits is declared, in `ports.ts`, and
7	 * handed over with the tile's box. Everything you can see is ours. That is why
8	 * only the library's bare
9	 * stylesheet is imported below and never its full one: the full one carries the
10	 * library's own look, and a tool that looks like the library it was built with
11	 * looks like a demo. A check in `npm run lint` fails the build if the full one
12	 * ever appears in this tree.
13	 *
14	 * Three things this file works out that no single wire could work out for
15	 * itself, because a wire cannot see where the other tiles are:
16	 *
17	 *   1. **How each wire is routed.** Most arrows join neighbouring columns and
18	 *      take the ordinary route. An arrow that skips a column would run straight
19	 *      through the tile in between and disappear behind it, so it is given a
20	 *      clear corridor to travel along instead; and the one arrow that runs
21	 *      backwards is sent over the top of the map, where there is nothing to
22	 *      cross.
23	 *   2. **The hover lens.** Point at a claim and everything not on its path —
24	 *      neither one of its causes nor one of the things it causes — drops to
25	 *      fifteen per cent.
26	 *   3. **Whether a wire's plate has room for its words.** Below the same zoom at
27	 *      which a tile switches to its summary, a plate's words would land under
28	 *      eleven pixels on the glass, so the plates go. Nothing is scaled down to
29	 *      dodge the rule.
30	 */

/**
 * The map: tiles, wires, panning and zooming.
 *
 * The drawing library owns four things and no more — panning, zooming, working
 * out what is under the pointer, and joining two ports with a stroke. It is not
 * told to find those ports: where each one sits is declared, in `ports.ts`, and
 * handed over with the tile's box. Everything you can see is ours. That is why
 * only the library's bare
 * stylesheet is imported below and never its full one: the full one carries the
 * library's own look, and a tool that looks like the library it was built with
 * looks like a demo. A check in `npm run lint` fails the build if the full one
 * ever appears in this tree.
 *
 * Three things this file works out that no single wire could work out for

 *      clear corridor to travel along instead; and the one arrow that runs
 *      backwards is sent over the top of the map, where there is nothing to
 *      cross.
 *   2. **The hover lens.** Point at a claim and everything not on its path —
 *      neither one of its causes nor one of the things it causes — drops to
 *      fifteen per cent.
 *   3. **Whether a wire's plate has room for its words.** Below the same zoom at
 *      which a tile switches to its summary, a plate's words would land under
 *      eleven pixels on the glass, so the plates go. Nothing is scaled down to
 *      dodge the rule.

1	/**
2	 * Where a tile's ports are, and the one place that says so.
3	 *
4	 * A **port** is the socket a wire attaches to. Every tile has four: a pair on
5	 * the left edge for arrows arriving and a pair on the right for arrows leaving,
6	 * and in each pair the upper socket is for an arrow that fires once and stays
7	 * fired, the lower for one that only holds while its cause holds. What a wire
8	 * means is visible at the socket before you follow it anywhere.
9	 *
10	 * **A port's place is declared, not discovered — and that is the whole point of
11	 * this file.** The drawing library draws a wire between two ports, and left to
12	 * itself it finds out where a port is by measuring the page, through the very
13	 * same browser notification a busy browser drops. A wire whose ends were never
14	 * measured is not drawn at all: the map holds every claim, in its place, and
15	 * says nothing about how they are joined, which is the wrong picture of the
16	 * argument and a silent one. #37 met the same dropped notification as tiles
17	 * that never appeared and answered it by telling the library each tile's box
18	 * outright. A box is not a port, so the wire half of it was left over. This is
19	 * the rest of the same answer: told its box *and* where its ports sit, a tile
20	 * can have its wires drawn on the first frame with nothing measured at all.
21	 *
22	 * So every number a port has is written here, and written **once**. The tile
23	 * puts these numbers straight onto the element it draws; the drawing library is
24	 * handed the same numbers; `wires/plates.ts` places a plate against them. This
25	 * file must never read a port's place back off the screen, and nothing else may
26	 * write one down a second time — two places that have to agree are two places
27	 * that one day will not.
28	 */
29	
30	import type { NodeHandle } from "@xyflow/react";
31	import { Position } from "@xyflow/react";
32	import type { LinkMode } from "../world";
33	import { TILE_WIDTH } from "./geometry";
34	
35	/**
36	 * How wide a port is, in pixels — one step of the eight-pixel grid the whole
37	 * interface sits on, doubled.
38	 *
39	 * It straddles the tile's edge, half in and half out, which is why it is twice
40	 * the standoff below.
41	 */
42	export const PORT_WIDTH = 16;
43	
44	/** How tall a port is, in pixels: enough for one bar, a gap and a second bar. */
45	export const PORT_HEIGHT = 6;
46	
47	/**
48	 * How far past the tile's edge a wire attaches, in pixels.
49	 *
50	 * A wire that met the tile flush would have its last few pixels drawn under the
51	 * tile's own outline. Eight pixels clear is one step of the grid.
52	 */
53	export const PORT_STANDOFF = 8;
54	
55	/**
56	 * How far down a tile each of the two sockets sits, as a share of its height.
57	 *
58	 * A share rather than a number of pixels, because a tile is as tall as its own
59	 * content: the pair has to stay evenly spaced about the middle on a tile of any
60	 * height. Read by `wires/plates.ts` as well, which has to know where a wire
61	 * will start before a single wire has been drawn.
62	 */
63	export const DOWN_THE_TILE: Readonly<Record<LinkMode, number>> = {
64	  trigger: 0.38,
65	  sustain: 0.62,
66	};
67	
68	/** What a port is called. These four names are what a wire names its ends by. */
69	export type PortId = "in-trigger" | "in-sustain" | "out-trigger" | "out-sustain";
70	
71	/** One socket on the edge of a tile. */
72	export interface Port {
73	  /** Its name, which is what a wire asks for. */
74	  readonly id: PortId;
75	  /** Whether wires leave from it or arrive at it. */
76	  readonly kind: "source" | "target";
77	  /** Which edge of the tile it is on. */
78	  readonly edge: Position;
79	  /** Which kind of push attaches here. Also what the socket is drawn as. */
80	  readonly mode: LinkMode;
81	}
82	
83	/**
84	 * The four ports every tile has, in the order they are drawn.
85	 *
86	 * Arriving before leaving, and within each pair the one that fires once before
87	 * the one that holds — the same top-to-bottom order the sockets are drawn in,
88	 * so the list reads the way the tile looks.
89	 */
90	export const PORTS: readonly Port[] = [
91	  { id: "in-trigger", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "trigger" },
92	  { id: "in-sustain", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "sustain" },
93	  { id: "out-trigger", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "trigger" },
94	  { id: "out-sustain", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "sustain" },
95	];
96	
97	/** A port's box, in the tile's own coordinates, with the tile's corner at zero. */
98	export interface PortBox {
99	  /** Its left edge. Negative on the left of a tile: the port straddles the edge. */
100	  readonly x: number;
101	  /** Its top edge. */
102	  readonly y: number;
103	  /** How wide it is. */
104	  readonly width: number;
105	  /** How tall it is. */
106	  readonly height: number;
107	}
108	
109	/**
110	 * Where this port sits on a tile of this height.
111	 *
112	 * The one piece of arithmetic in this file, and every other number here and in
113	 * the tile comes out of it. The box straddles the tile's edge so that the wire
114	 * attaches a clear eight pixels outside it, and it is centred on the share of
115	 * the height the socket sits at.
116	 *
117	 * @param height How tall the tile is — the same number the layout reserved for
118	 *   it and the same number the tile is drawn at. A tile that grew a line
119	 *   because an edit touched it moves its ports down with it, and this is where
120	 *   that happens.
121	 * @param port Which of the four.
122	 */
123	export function portBox(height: number, port: Port): PortBox {
124	  return {
125	    x: port.edge === Position.Left ? -PORT_STANDOFF : TILE_WIDTH + PORT_STANDOFF - PORT_WIDTH,
126	    y: height * DOWN_THE_TILE[port.mode] - PORT_HEIGHT / 2,
127	    width: PORT_WIDTH,
128	    height: PORT_HEIGHT,
129	  };
130	}
131	
132	/**
133	 * Every port of a tile this tall, in the shape the drawing library takes them.
134	 *
135	 * Handed over with the tile's box, so that the library knows where both ends of
136	 * every wire are before it has measured anything. It keeps measuring afterwards
137	 * and rebuilds these from what it measures; the numbers are the same numbers,
138	 * because the tile was drawn from them.
139	 *
140	 * @param height How tall the tile is.
141	 */
142	export function portsOf(height: number): NodeHandle[] {
143	  return PORTS.map((port) => ({
144	    id: port.id,
145	    type: port.kind,
146	    position: port.edge,
147	    ...portBox(height, port),
148	  }));
149	}
150	
151	/**
152	 * Which port a wire of this kind leaves from, and which it arrives at.
153	 *
154	 * @param mode Whether the push fires once or has to keep holding.
155	 */
156	export function portsForAWire(mode: LinkMode): {
157	  readonly source: PortId;
158	  readonly target: PortId;
159	} {
160	  return mode === "sustain"
161	    ? { source: "out-sustain", target: "in-sustain" }
162	    : { source: "out-trigger", target: "in-trigger" };
163	}

27	 * that one day will not.
28	 */
29	
30	import type { NodeHandle } from "@xyflow/react";
31	import { Position } from "@xyflow/react";
32	import type { LinkMode } from "../world";
33	import { TILE_WIDTH } from "./geometry";
34	
35	/**
36	 * How wide a port is, in pixels — one step of the eight-pixel grid the whole
37	 * interface sits on, doubled.
38	 *
39	 * It straddles the tile's edge, half in and half out, which is why it is twice
40	 * the standoff below.
41	 */
42	export const PORT_WIDTH = 16;
43	
44	/** How tall a port is, in pixels: enough for one bar, a gap and a second bar. */
45	export const PORT_HEIGHT = 6;
46	
47	/**
48	 * How far past the tile's edge a wire attaches, in pixels.
49	 *
50	 * A wire that met the tile flush would have its last few pixels drawn under the
51	 * tile's own outline. Eight pixels clear is one step of the grid.
52	 */
53	export const PORT_STANDOFF = 8;
54	
55	/**
56	 * How far down a tile each of the two sockets sits, as a share of its height.
57	 *
58	 * A share rather than a number of pixels, because a tile is as tall as its own
59	 * content: the pair has to stay evenly spaced about the middle on a tile of any
60	 * height. Read by `wires/plates.ts` as well, which has to know where a wire
61	 * will start before a single wire has been drawn.
62	 */
63	export const DOWN_THE_TILE: Readonly<Record<LinkMode, number>> = {
64	  trigger: 0.38,
65	  sustain: 0.62,
66	};
67	
68	/** What a port is called. These four names are what a wire names its ends by. */
69	export type PortId = "in-trigger" | "in-sustain" | "out-trigger" | "out-sustain";
70	
71	/** One socket on the edge of a tile. */
72	export interface Port {
73	  /** Its name, which is what a wire asks for. */
74	  readonly id: PortId;
75	  /** Whether wires leave from it or arrive at it. */
76	  readonly kind: "source" | "target";
77	  /** Which edge of the tile it is on. */
78	  readonly edge: Position;
79	  /** Which kind of push attaches here. Also what the socket is drawn as. */
80	  readonly mode: LinkMode;
81	}
82	
83	/**
84	 * The four ports every tile has, in the order they are drawn.
85	 *
86	 * Arriving before leaving, and within each pair the one that fires once before
87	 * the one that holds — the same top-to-bottom order the sockets are drawn in,
88	 * so the list reads the way the tile looks.
89	 */
90	export const PORTS: readonly Port[] = [
91	  { id: "in-trigger", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "trigger" },
92	  { id: "in-sustain", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "sustain" },
93	  { id: "out-trigger", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "trigger" },
94	  { id: "out-sustain", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "sustain" },
95	];
96	
97	/** A port's box, in the tile's own coordinates, with the tile's corner at zero. */
98	export interface PortBox {
99	  /** Its left edge. Negative on the left of a tile: the port straddles the edge. */
100	  readonly x: number;
101	  /** Its top edge. */
102	  readonly y: number;
103	  /** How wide it is. */
104	  readonly width: number;
105	  /** How tall it is. */
106	  readonly height: number;
107	}
108	
109	/**
110	 * Where this port sits on a tile of this height.
111	 *
112	 * The one piece of arithmetic in this file, and every other number here and in
113	 * the tile comes out of it. The box straddles the tile's edge so that the wire
114	 * attaches a clear eight pixels outside it, and it is centred on the share of
115	 * the height the socket sits at.
116	 *
117	 * @param height How tall the tile is — the same number the layout reserved for
118	 *   it and the same number the tile is drawn at. A tile that grew a line
119	 *   because an edit touched it moves its ports down with it, and this is where
120	 *   that happens.
121	 * @param port Which of the four.
122	 */
123	export function portBox(height: number, port: Port): PortBox {
124	  return {
125	    x: port.edge === Position.Left ? -PORT_STANDOFF : TILE_WIDTH + PORT_STANDOFF - PORT_WIDTH,
126	    y: height * DOWN_THE_TILE[port.mode] - PORT_HEIGHT / 2,
127	    width: PORT_WIDTH,
128	    height: PORT_HEIGHT,
129	  };
130	}
131	
132	/**
133	 * Every port of a tile this tall, in the shape the drawing library takes them.
134	 *
135	 * Handed over with the tile's box, so that the library knows where both ends of
136	 * every wire are before it has measured anything. It keeps measuring afterwards
137	 * and rebuilds these from what it measures; the numbers are the same numbers,
138	 * because the tile was drawn from them.
139	 *
140	 * @param height How tall the tile is.
141	 */
142	export function portsOf(height: number): NodeHandle[] {
143	  return PORTS.map((port) => ({
144	    id: port.id,
145	    type: port.kind,
146	    position: port.edge,
147	    ...portBox(height, port),
148	  }));
149	}
150	
151	/**
152	 * Which port a wire of this kind leaves from, and which it arrives at.
153	 *
154	 * @param mode Whether the push fires once or has to keep holding.
155	 */
156	export function portsForAWire(mode: LinkMode): {
157	  readonly source: PortId;
158	  readonly target: PortId;
159	} {
160	  return mode === "sustain"
161	    ? { source: "out-sustain", target: "in-sustain" }
162	    : { source: "out-trigger", target: "in-trigger" };
163	}
</system-reminder>

input.content:
fix(canvas): a tile says where its ports are, so a wire is drawn before anything is measured

**The root.** A wire is drawn between two ports — the sockets on a tile's
edges — and the drawing library refuses to draw one whose ports it cannot
place. Left to itself it places them by measuring the rendered tile, through
the same `ResizeObserver` notification a busy browser abandons when too many
fall due in one frame; an abandoned one is never delivered. #37 met that
notification as tiles that never appeared and answered it by telling the
library each tile's box outright. A box is not a port, so the wire half was
left over, and the arrow stayed off the glass for the life of the page.

**Measured three ways.** Drop every tile's notification and keep the glass's:
seven tiles drawn, none hidden, twenty-eight ports on the glass, and not one
arrow. Drop only the insurance premium's: the two arrows touching it go, and
only those. Drop only the strait's: its three go. And in the wild, on ports
nobody else on this machine held, with sixteen busy loops alongside — one run
in two hundred at six workers lost `H->C` exactly that way, with every tile in
place.

**One rule, not two: a tile is told its box and where its ports sit, from the
one place that worked them out.** `graph/ports.ts` is that place. It holds the
four ports every tile has, their two shares of the tile's height, their size
and their standoff, and the one piece of arithmetic that turns a height into
four boxes. `toFlow` hands those boxes to the library beside `initialWidth`
and `initialHeight`; `Tile.tsx` writes the very same numbers onto the elements
it draws; `wires/plates.ts` reads the shares and the standoff from there
instead of writing them down a third time. Nothing measures a port, nothing
waits for a measurement, and nothing polls: `isNodeInitialized` accepts a
declared port alongside a declared width, so both ends of every arrow are
known on the first frame.

**Declared and measured are the same numbers, and that matters.** The library
keeps measuring, and `adoptUserNodes` rebuilds a node's port bounds from what
was declared every time the map is redrawn — so a declared offset that
disagreed with the measured one would jump a wire's ends back and forth on
every hover. Driven through the installed library with the measurement
simulated at the browser's own layout unit, one sixty-fourth of a pixel, the
worst move is 0.0056 px. The ports render where they rendered before, to a
hundredth of a pixel, and `socketsFor` returns the numbers it returned before,
unchanged.

**What this replaces.** A hook that asked the library to re-measure every tile
eight times a second, on the state of `useNodesInitialized`. That flag is
permanently false in this app — the canvas builds new node objects on every
change, so the library's `measured` is discarded and, with neither default
nodes nor an `onNodesChange`, never written back — so the asking never stopped
and the fix worked only because it never stopped. The hook is gone.

The end-to-end suite now checks every arrow by name on the stored example, not
only the one an edit is made to; a map drawing six of eight was invisible to
it. `test_the_arrows_are_drawn_when_the_browser_drops_a_size_notification`
keeps its shim and now asserts the same eight, so it says *nothing changes*
rather than *something was drawn*.

test_a_port_is_placed_from_the_height_the_box_was_declared_at
test_a_declared_port_is_where_the_tile_draws_it
test_a_wire_attaches_where_the_plate_expects_it
